'''Ziheng Yang''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society#Fellows|FRS]] ({{zh|c=杨子恒}}; born 1 November 1964) is a British [[biologist]].  He holds the R.A. Fisher Chair of Statistical Genetics<ref>{{cite web |title=Genetics, Evolution and Environment |url=http://www.ucl.ac.uk/gee/gee-news-publication/20100410-1 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160628131555/http://www.ucl.ac.uk/gee/gee-news-publication/20100410-1 |archive-date=28 June 2016 |access-date=23 June 2017 |website=Ucl.ac.uk}}</ref> at [[University College London]],<ref name="WW">‘YANG, Prof. Ziheng’, Who's Who 2011, A & C Black, 2011; online edn, Oxford University Press, Dec 2010; online edn, Oct 2010 [http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U151365, accessed 11 May 2011]{{subscription required}}</ref> and is the Director of R.A. Fisher Centre for Computational Biology at UCL.  He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 2006.<ref name="WW" />

==Academic career==
Yang graduated from [[Gansu Agricultural University]] with a BSc in 1984, and from [[Beijing Agricultural University]] with a MSc in 1987, and PhD in 1992.<ref>{{cite web |title=Iris View Profile |url=https://iris.ucl.ac.uk/research/personal?upi=ZYANG48 |access-date=23 June 2017 |website=Iris.ucl.ac.uk |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303221941/https://iris.ucl.ac.uk/research/personal?upi=ZYANG48 |archive-date=3 March 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref>

After the PhD, he worked as a postdoctoral researcher in Department of Zoology, University of Cambridge (1992–93), The Natural History Museum (London) (1993–94), Pennsylvania State University (1994–95), and University of California at Berkeley (1995–97), before taking up a faculty position in Department of Biology, University College London.  He was a Lecturer (1997), Reader (2000), and then Professor (2001) in the same department.  He was appointed to the R.A. Fisher Chair in Statistical Genetics in UCL in 2010.

Yang held a number of visiting appointments.  He was a Visiting Associate Professor at
Institute of Statistical Mathematics (Tokyo, 1997–8), a visiting professor at University of
Tokyo (2007–08), Institute of Zoology in Beijing (2010–1), Peking
University (2010), National Institute of Genetics, Mishima, Japan
(2011), and Swiss Institute of Technology (ETH), Zurich (2011).  In 2008–2011, he was the Changjiang Chair Professor at [[Sun Yat-sen University]], with an award from the [[Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China|Ministry of Education]] of China.  From 2016 to 2019, he was a visiting professor at National Institute of Genetics, Japan.  In 2017–8, he was a Radcliffe Fellow at Harvard University's Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study.<ref name="Radcliffe_Institute_for_Advanced_Study_at_Harvard_University-1">{{Cite web |title=Ziheng Yang |url=https://www.radcliffe.harvard.edu/people/ziheng-yang |access-date=1 December 2017 |website=Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study at Harvard University |language=en}}</ref>

==Work in molecular evolution and phylogenetics==
Yang developed a number of statistical models and methods in the 1990s, which have been implemented in maximum likelihood and Bayesian software programs for phylogenetic analysis of DNA and protein sequence data.  Two decades ago, Felsenstein had described the pruning algorithm for calculating the likelihood on a phylogeny.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Felsenstein |first=Joe |date=1973 |title=Maximum likelihood and minimum-steps methods for estimating evolutionary trees from data on discrete characters |journal=Syst. Zool. |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=240–249 |doi=10.2307/2412304 |jstor=2412304}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Felsenstein |first=Joe |date=1981 |title=Evolutionary trees from DNA sequences: a maximum likelihood approach |journal=J. Mol. Evol. |volume=17 |issue=6 |pages=368–376 |bibcode=1981JMolE..17..368F |doi=10.1007/bf01734359 |pmid=7288891 |s2cid=8024924}}</ref>  However, the assumed model of character change was simple and, for example, does not account for variable rates among sites in the sequence.  By illustrating the power of statistical models to accommodate major features of the evolutionary process and to address important evolutionary questions using molecular sequence data, the models and methods Yang developed had a major impact on the cladistic-statistical controversy at the time and played a major role in the transformation of molecular phylogenetics.

Yang developed a maximum likelihood model of gamma-distributed evolutionary rate variation among sites in the sequence in 1993–4.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yang |first=Ziheng |date=1993 |title=Maximum-likelihood estimation of phylogeny from DNA sequences when substitution rates differ over sites |journal=Mol. Biol. Evol. |volume=10 |issue=6 |pages=1396–1401 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.molbev.a040082 |pmid=8277861 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Z |year=1994 |title=Maximum likelihood phylogenetic estimation from DNA sequences with variable rates over sites: approximate methods |journal=J Mol Evol |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=306–314 |bibcode=1994JMolE..39..306Y |doi=10.1007/bf00160154 |pmid=7932792 |s2cid=17911050}}</ref>  The models he developed for combined analysis of heterogeneous data <ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Yang Z, Lauder IJ, Lin HJ |date=1995 |title=Molecular evolution of the hepatitis B virus genome |journal=J. Mol. Evol. |volume=41 |issue=5 |pages=587–596 |bibcode=1995JMolE..41..587Y |doi=10.1007/bf00175817 |pmid=7490773 |s2cid=9176917}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yang Z. |date=1996 |title=Maximum-likelihood models for combined analyses of multiple sequence data |journal=J. Mol. Evol. |volume=42 |issue=5 |pages=587–596 |bibcode=1996JMolE..42..587Y |doi=10.1007/bf02352289 |pmid=8662011 |s2cid=12660243}}</ref> are later known as partition models and mixture models.

Together with [[Nick Goldman]], Yang developed the codon model of nucleotide substitution in 1994.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Goldman N, Yang Z |date=1994 |title=A codon-based model of nucleotide substitution for protein-coding DNA sequences |journal=Mol Biol Evol |volume=11 |issue=5 |pages=725–736 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.molbev.a040153 |pmid=7968486 |doi-access=free}}</ref>  This formed the basis for phylogenetic analysis of protein-coding genes to detect molecular adaptation or Darwinian evolution at the molecular level.  A stream of papers followed this to extend the original model to accommodate variable selection pressures (measured by the dN/dS ratio) among evolutionary lineages or among sites in the protein sequence.  The ''branch models'' allow different branches to have different dN/dS ratios among branches on the tree and can be used to test for positive selection affecting particular lineages.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yang |first=Ziheng |date=1998 |title=Likelihood ratio tests for detecting positive selection and application to primate lysozyme evolution |journal=Mol. Biol. Evol. |volume=15 |issue=5 |pages=568–573 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.molbev.a025957 |pmid=9580986 |doi-access=free}}</ref>  The ''site models'' allow different selective pressures on different amino acids in the protein and can be used to test for positive selection affecting only a few amino acid sites.<ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Nielsen, R. |author2=Yang, Z. |date=1998 |title=Likelihood models for detecting positively selected amino acid sites and applications to the HIV-1 envelope gene |journal=Genetics |volume=148 |issue=3 |pages=929–936 |doi=10.1093/genetics/148.3.929 |pmc=1460041 |pmid=9539414}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Yang, Z. |author2=Nielsen, R. |author3=Goldman, N. |author4=Pedersen, A.-M.K. |date=2000 |title=Codon-substitution models for heterogeneous selection pressure at amino acid sites |journal=Genetics |volume=155 |issue=1 |pages=431–449 |doi=10.1093/genetics/155.1.431 |pmc=1461088 |pmid=10790415}}</ref><ref name="Yang 1107–1118">{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Ziheng |last2=Wong |first2=Wendy S. W. |last3=Nielsen |first3=Rasmus |date=1 April 2005 |title=Bayes Empirical Bayes Inference of Amino Acid Sites Under Positive Selection |url=https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/22/4/1107/1083468 |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |volume=22 |issue=4 |pages=1107–1118 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msi097 |issn=0737-4038 |pmid=15689528 |doi-access=free |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171112032123/https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/22/4/1107/1083468 |archive-date=12 November 2017 |access-date=11 November 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>  And the ''branch-site models'' attempt to detect positive selection that affects only a few amino acid sites along pre-specific lineages.<ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Yang, Z. |author2=Nielsen, R. |date=2002 |title=Codon-substitution models for detecting molecular adaptation at individual sites along specific lineages |journal=Mol. Biol. Evol. |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=908–917 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.molbev.a004148 |hdl=1813/32161 |pmid=12032247 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Yang 1107–1118"/>  A recent book reviews the recent developments in this area.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Codon evolution : mechanisms and models |date=2012 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780199601165 |editor1=Cannarozzi, Gina M. |location=Oxford |oclc=784949340 |editor2=Schneider, Adrian}}</ref>

Yang developed the statistical (empirical Bayes) method for reconstructing ancestral sequences in 1995.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Yang Z, Kumar S, Nei M |date=1995 |title=A new method of inference of ancestral nucleotide and amino acid sequences |journal=Genetics |volume=141 |issue=4 |pages=1641–1650 |doi=10.1093/genetics/141.4.1641 |pmc=1206894 |pmid=8601501}}</ref> Compared with the parsimony method of ancestral sequence reconstruction (that is, the Fitch–Hartigan algorithm),<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fitch |first=Walter M. |date=1971 |title=Toward defining the course of evolution: minimum change for a specific tree topology |journal=Syst. Zool. |volume=20 |issue=4 |pages=406–416 |doi=10.2307/2412116 |jstor=2412116}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hartigan, J.A. |date=1973 |title=Minimum evolution fits to a given tree |journal=Biometrics |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=53–65 |doi=10.2307/2529676 |jstor=2529676}}</ref> this has the advantages of using branch-length information and of providing a probabilistic assessment of the reconstruction uncertainties.

Together with Bruce Rannala, Yang introduced Bayesian statistics into molecular phylogenetics in 1996.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Rannala B, Yang Z |date=1996 |title=Probability distribution of molecular evolutionary trees: a new method of phylogenetic inference |journal=J. Mol. Evol. |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=304–311 |bibcode=1996JMolE..43..304R |doi=10.1007/bf02338839 |pmid=8703097 |s2cid=8269826}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Yang Z, Rannala B |date=1997 |title=Bayesian phylogenetic inference using DNA sequences: a Markov chain Monte Carlo Method |journal=Mol. Biol. Evol. |volume=14 |issue=7 |pages=717–724 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.molbev.a025811 |pmid=9214744 |doi-access=free}}</ref>  The Bayesian is now one of the most popular statistical methodologies used in modeling and inference in molecular phylogenetics.  Recent exciting developments in Bayesian phylogenetics are summarized in an edited book<ref>{{Cite book |title=Bayesian phylogenetics : methods, algorithms, and applications |date=27 May 2014 |publisher=Chapman & Hall/CRC |isbn=9781466500792 |editor1=Chen, Ming-Hui |location=Boca Raton |oclc=881387408 |editor2=Kuo, Lynn |editor3=Lewis, Paul O.}}</ref> and in chapter 8 of Yang's book.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ziheng |first=Yang |title=Molecular evolution : a statistical approach |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2014 |isbn=9780199602605 |edition=First |location=Oxford |oclc=869346345}}</ref>

Yang and Rannala also developed the multispecies coalescent model,<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Rannala B, Yang Z |date=2003 |title=Bayes estimation of species divergence times and ancestral population sizes using DNA sequences from multiple loci |journal=Genetics |volume=164 |issue=4 |pages=1645–1656 |doi=10.1093/genetics/164.4.1645 |pmc=1462670 |pmid=12930768}}</ref> which has emerged as the natural framework for comparative analysis of genomic sequence data from multiple species, incorporating the coalescent process in both modern species and extinct ancestors.  The model has been used to estimate the species tree despite gene tree heterogeneity among genomic regions,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Ziheng |last2=Rannala |first2=Bruce |date=1 December 2014 |title=Unguided Species Delimitation Using DNA Sequence Data from Multiple Loci |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |volume=31 |issue=12 |pages=3125–3135 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msu279 |issn=0737-4038 |pmc=4245825 |pmid=25274273}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rannala |first1=Bruce |last2=Yang |first2=Ziheng |date=1 September 2017 |title=Efficient Bayesian Species Tree Inference under the Multispecies Coalescent |url=https://academic.oup.com/sysbio/article/66/5/823/2805857 |journal=Systematic Biology |volume=66 |issue=5 |pages=823–842 |arxiv=1512.03843 |doi=10.1093/sysbio/syw119 |issn=1063-5157 |pmc=8562347 |pmid=28053140 |s2cid=3554064 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180712120146/https://academic.oup.com/sysbio/article/66/5/823/2805857 |archive-date=12 July 2018 |access-date=11 November 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Xu |first1=Bo |last2=Yang |first2=Ziheng |date=1 December 2016 |title=Challenges in Species Tree Estimation Under the Multispecies Coalescent Model |url=http://www.genetics.org/content/204/4/1353 |journal=Genetics |language=en |volume=204 |issue=4 |pages=1353–1368 |doi=10.1534/genetics.116.190173 |issn=0016-6731 |pmc=5161269 |pmid=27927902 |bibcode=2016Genet.204.1353X |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171111095324/http://www.genetics.org/content/204/4/1353 |archive-date=11 November 2017 |access-date=11 November 2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> and to delimit/identify species.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Ziheng |last2=Rannala |first2=Bruce |date=18 May 2010 |title=Bayesian species delimitation using multilocus sequence data |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=107 |issue=20 |pages=9264–9269 |bibcode=2010PNAS..107.9264Y |doi=10.1073/pnas.0913022107 |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=2889046 |pmid=20439743 |doi-access=free}}</ref>  Yang champions Bayesian parametric inference under full likelihood models, using Markov chain Monte Carlo to average over gene trees (gene genealogies), accommodating phylogenetic uncertainties.<ref name=":0" />

Yang maintains the program package PAML (for Phylogenetic Analysis by Maximum Likelihood)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yang |first=Ziheng |date=2007 |title=PAML 4: Phylogenetic analysis by maximum likelihood |journal=Mol. Biol. Evol. |volume=24 |issue=8 |pages=1586–1591 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msm088 |pmid=17483113 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and the Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo program BPP (for Bayesian Phylogenetics and Phylogeography).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yang |first=Ziheng |date=1 October 2015 |title=The BPP program for species tree estimation and species delimitation |url=https://academic.oup.com/cz/article/61/5/854/1821090 |journal=Current Zoology |volume=61 |issue=5 |pages=854–865 |doi=10.1093/czoolo/61.5.854 |issn=1674-5507 |doi-access=free |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171111103944/https://academic.oup.com/cz/article/61/5/854/1821090 |archive-date=11 November 2017 |access-date=11 November 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Work in principles of statistical inference and computational statistics==
Yang studied the star tree paradox, which is that Bayesian model selection produces spuriously high posterior probabilities for the binary trees if the data are simulated under the star tree.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Ziheng |last2=Rannala |first2=Bruce |last3=Lewis |first3=Paul |date=1 June 2005 |title=Branch-Length Prior Influences Bayesian Posterior Probability of Phylogeny |journal=Systematic Biology |language=en |volume=54 |issue=3 |pages=455–470 |doi=10.1080/10635150590945313 |issn=1063-5157 |pmid=16012111 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Yang |first=Ziheng |date=1 August 2007 |title=Fair-Balance Paradox, Star-tree Paradox, and Bayesian Phylogenetics |url=https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/24/8/1639/2925627 |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |volume=24 |issue=8 |pages=1639–1655 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msm081 |issn=0737-4038 |pmid=17488737 |doi-access=free |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171111102412/https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/24/8/1639/2925627 |archive-date=11 November 2017 |access-date=11 November 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>   A simpler case showing similar behaviours is the fair-coin paradox.<ref name=":1" />  The work suggests that Bayesian model selection may produce unpleasant polarized behavior supporting one model with full force while rejecting the others, when the competing models are all misspecified and equally wrong.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Ziheng |last2=Zhu |first2=Tianqi |date=5 February 2018 |title=Bayesian selection of misspecified models is overconfident and may cause spurious posterior probabilities for phylogenetic trees |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=115 |issue=8 |pages=1854–1859 |bibcode=2018PNAS..115.1854Y |doi=10.1073/pnas.1712673115 |pmc=5828583 |pmid=29432193 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Yang has worked extensively on Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, deriving many Metropolis-Hastings algorithms in Bayesian phylogenetics.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ziheng |first=Yang |title=Molecular evolution : a statistical approach |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2014 |isbn=9780199602612 |edition=First |location=Oxford |oclc=869346345}}</ref>  A study examining the efficiency of simple MCMC proposals revealed that the well-studied Gaussian random-walk move is less efficient than the simple uniform random-walk move, which is in turn less efficient than the Bactrian moves, bimodal moves that suppress values very close to the current state.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Ziheng |last2=Rodríguez |first2=Carlos E. |date=26 November 2013 |title=Searching for efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo proposal kernels |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=110 |issue=48 |pages=19307–19312 |bibcode=2013PNAS..11019307Y |doi=10.1073/pnas.1311790110 |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=3845170 |pmid=24218600 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Professional activities==
Yang taught in Woods Hole Workshop on Molecular Evolution.

He was a co-organizer of the Royal Society Discussion Meeting on "Statistical and computational challenges in molecular phylogenetics and evolution" on 28–29 April 2008,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Statistical and computational challenges in molecular phylogenetics and evolution |url=https://royalsociety.org/science-events-and-lectures/2008/molecular-phylogenetics/ |website=Royal Society |access-date=28 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201030810/https://royalsociety.org/science-events-and-lectures/2008/molecular-phylogenetics/ |archive-date=1 December 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref> and the Royal Society Discussion Meeting on "Dating species divergence using rocks and clocks", on 9–10 November 2015.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dating species divergences using rocks and clocks |url=https://royalsociety.org/science-events-and-lectures/2015/11/dating-species-divergences/ |website=Royal Society |access-date=28 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201072125/https://royalsociety.org/science-events-and-lectures/2015/11/dating-species-divergences/ |archive-date=1 December 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Since 2009, he has been a co-organizer of an annual workshop on Computational Molecular Evolution (CoME), which has been running in Sanger/Hinxton in odd years and in Hiraklion, Crete in even years.[http://abacus.gene.ucl.ac.uk/meetings/CoME/]{{Dead link|date=September 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}

He also organized and taught in a number of workshops in Beijing, China.
